blurb: Why AI confidently makes things up, how to catch it, and what researchers find when they look inside a model's "brain".

steps.p: A model learned to produce likely-sounding text. A made-up fact in the right style sounds just as likely as a real one — so it can come out just as confidently.
steps.analogy: A student who has read a lot and bluffs fluently when they don't actually know.

steps.p: Most tests give marks for right answers and nothing for "I don't know". So guessing scores better than admitting doubt, and models learn to guess.
Things seen thousands of times in training (Paris is in France) stick. Things seen once or twice (an obscure person's birthday) are hazy, so the model fills gaps.

visual.x: How often a fact appears in training
visual.caption: Illustration: rarer facts, more made-up answers.

steps.h: Hard to tell from the outside
steps.p: A hallucination reads exactly like a true answer — same tone, same confidence, sometimes with fake sources.
Base models are fairly well calibrated — their confidence matches how often they're right. Post-training to be helpful and decisive can weaken that.

cards.q: A 2025 OpenAI paper argued one key cause of hallucination is that tests…
options: Reward guessing over admitting uncertainty, with no penalty for wrong answers
cards.hint: Look at the comparison in step 2.
cards.why: Guessing pays. If wrong answers cost nothing and "I don't know" scores zero, a model maximising its score learns to always guess. Penalising confident errors would change that.

cards.q: Which is a model more likely to make up?
options: The birth year of an obscure local politician
How many days are in a week
cards.why: The obscure fact. Rarely mentioned facts are weakly learned, so the model fills the gap with a plausible guess.

cards.title: In 2023, US lawyers were fined for submitting a court filing citing cases ChatGPT had invented.
cards.detail: In Mata v. Avianca, the judge found six cited decisions didn't exist. The lawyers had even asked ChatGPT whether the cases were real — and it said yes.

cards.statement: Hallucinations only happen on obscure topics.
cards.why: False. They're more common there, but models also invent quotes, sources, numbers and steps in reasoning on familiar topics.

cards.statement: OpenAI reported that GPT-4's base model was better calibrated about its confidence than the model after post-training.
cards.why: True. The GPT-4 report showed post-training hurt calibration: the chatbot's confidence matched its accuracy less well than the raw model's.

steps.p: Paste the document or connect search, and tell it to answer only from that. Answering from text in front of it is far more reliable than from memory.
Explicitly allow it to say it isn't sure or that the document doesn't say. Models bluff less when told bluffing is worse than admitting a gap.
Ask it to quote the exact sentence supporting each claim. Made-up claims have nothing to quote, so they stand out.
steps.analogy: "Show me where it says that" — the question every good teacher asks.

steps.p: Ask the same question several times. Real knowledge stays consistent; invented details change each time.
Numbers, names, dates, quotes and citations are where invented details hide. Verify those before you rely on them.

cards.q: Which instruction most directly helps you catch made-up claims in a document summary?
options: "Quote the sentence from the document that supports each claim"
cards.hint: Show me where it says that.
cards.why: Ask for quotes. You can search the document for each quote. A claim with no real supporting sentence is a red flag.

cards.statement: A more fluent and detailed answer is more likely to be true.
cards.why: False. Models are fluent either way. Extra detail can actually mean extra invented specifics.

options: Asking several times and checking whether the answers agree
cards.hint: Look at the comparison in step 4.
cards.why: Consistency. If the model really knows something, repeated answers match. Wildly varying answers suggest it's making it up.

cards.title: Meta's "Chain-of-Verification" reduced hallucinations by having the model fact-check itself in separate steps.
cards.detail: It drafts an answer, writes checking questions, answers each one independently without seeing the draft, then revises. Independence stops it simply repeating its own mistakes.

cards.title: Check numbers and names
cards.body: Invented details cluster in specifics: statistics, dates, names, quotes and references.
cards.challenge: Next time an AI gives you a statistic or quote, search for its original source before using it.

steps.p: We know every number in a model, but not what they mean. Interpretability research tries to work out what's going on inside.
steps.analogy: Having a full wiring diagram of a brain but no idea which wires mean "dog".

steps.p: You might hope each neuron means one thing. Instead most respond to a jumble of unrelated things — say, Korean text, legal terms and cat photos.
Models have to represent far more ideas than they have neurons, so they store them as overlapping combinations — many ideas squeezed into the same space.
A sparse autoencoder learns a big list of "features" so that each moment's activity is a few features added together. Many features turn out to be clean, readable ideas.

items: A few clear features: bridge, code bug, sarcasm

steps.p: Find a feature and you can turn it up or down, and watch the model's behaviour change — proof the feature really matters.

cards.statement: Each neuron in a large language model usually represents one clean, understandable idea.
cards.why: False. Most neurons respond to many unrelated things. That's why researchers look for features — combinations of neurons — instead.

options: Store more ideas than they have neurons by overlapping them
Run on two GPUs at once
Have two copies of every layer
cards.hint: Many ideas squeezed into the same space.
cards.why: Overlapping storage. Since most ideas are rarely active together, the model can pack them into shared neurons with little confusion.

cards.title: Anthropic made Claude believe it was the Golden Gate Bridge by turning up one internal feature.
cards.detail: In May 2024 researchers found a feature for the bridge and amplified it. "Golden Gate Claude" steered nearly every conversation to the bridge — even describing itself as it.

cards.q: Anthropic's 2024 research found millions of features in a Claude model, including…
options: Abstract ones, like for code bugs or deception, that work across languages and images
cards.why: Abstract, cross-language features. A "Golden Gate Bridge" feature fired for English, other languages and photos — evidence of real concepts, not just word patterns.

cards.q: A sparse autoencoder is trained to…
options: Rebuild a model's activity from a few active features out of a large dictionary
cards.why: Explain activity with few features. Forcing only a few features to be active at once pushes each one to mean something specific.

steps.p: Features connect into circuits: chains of features that together carry out a step of thinking.
Ask "What's the capital of the state containing Dallas?" and researchers can watch "Texas" light up inside before "Austin" — a real middle step.
When writing a rhyming couplet, Claude picks the rhyming word for the end of the line first, then writes the line to reach it.
steps.analogy: Like a poet who decides on the punchline before writing the setup.

steps.p: A probe is a simple test trained on a model's internal activity to check whether some information — like "is this statement true?" — is in there.
These are glimpses of small pieces. Fully explaining how a frontier model reaches a decision is far beyond current methods.

cards.q: When writing a rhyming couplet, research found Claude…
options: Chose the rhyming word in advance and wrote the line to reach it
cards.why: It plans ahead. Even though it outputs one token at a time, it had already settled on the ending — evidence of planning inside.

cards.statement: Adding a direction to a model's internal activity can change its behaviour without any retraining.
cards.why: True. This is called steering — like Golden Gate Claude. It changes behaviour for as long as the nudge is applied.

options: A simple test trained on a model's activity to see what information it contains
A tool that physically opens a GPU
cards.why: A simple detector. If a tiny classifier can read, say, "true or false" from the activity, that information is encoded there.

cards.title: Models seem to store "true" versus "false" along a single direction in their internal activity.
cards.detail: Research such as "The Geometry of Truth" (2023) found true and false statements separate cleanly, and pushing along that direction could flip how the model treats a statement.

cards.statement: Interpretability research can already fully explain how frontier models make their decisions.
cards.why: False. It can explain specific behaviours in pieces. A full account of a frontier model's decisions is still far away.
